segments.text: You will hear two psychology students discussing the effects of the order in which the children in a family are born.
First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
Ed, how are you getting on with the reading for our presentation next week?
Well, okay, Ruth, but there's so much of it.
I know. I hadn't realised birth order was such a popular area of research.
But the stuff on birth order and personality is mostly unreliable. From what I've been reading, a lot of the claims are just stereotypes.
Okay, but that's an interesting point. We could start by outlining what previous research has shown.
There are studies going back over 100 years.
Yeah, so we could just run through some of the typical traits.
Oldest children are generally less well-adjusted but are thought to be good at nurturing.
Middle children are easier to get on with and eager to please.
Youngest children are supposed to be sociable and confident, but that's not always true.
There have also been studies on twins, suggesting they may be shy in social situations.
Only children are often described as loners who expect attention.
Children with much older siblings may grow up faster and become more independent.
What was the problem with most of these studies?
Data was often collected from only one sibling, which reduced reliability.
Some studies found that intelligence scores decline slightly from oldest to youngest child.
But many didn't consider family size and socio-economic status.
Oldest children benefit from teaching younger siblings, which improves their own learning.
Sibling rivalry can also help develop confidence and resilience.
Despite conflicts, siblings usually learn to coexist and develop social skills.
